Confidence Interval for a Mean Under Two-Phase Sampling With a Proxy Measurement

Source: R/ci_two_phase.R
ci_two_phase.Rd

The confidence interval for the population mean of a target measurement that is costly to obtain and so is observed on only a random subsample of units, when an inexpensive proxy measurement is observed on every unit of a larger pool. The design is two-phase, or double, sampling (Neyman, 1938): the first phase draws the pool and measures the proxy on all of it, and the second draws a simple random subsample of the pool, the labeled units, and measures the target on them. The regression estimator of the target mean, the row mean_Y of the table, $$\hat{\mu}_Y = \bar y_n + \hat b\,(\bar x_M - \bar x_n),$$ adjusts the labeled units' target mean \(\bar y_n\) by how far their proxy mean \(\bar x_n\) sits from the proxy mean of the whole pool \(\bar x_M\), through the least squares slope \(\hat b\) of the target on the proxy in the labeled units. When the two measurements are strongly correlated, the interval is much narrower than the one the labeled units give alone, which is the point of the design.

Usage

ci_two_phase(
  y,
  x,
  x_unlabeled,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  method = c("regression", "prediction_powered"),
  cluster = NULL,
  cluster_unlabeled = NULL
)

Arguments

y

The target measurement on the \(n\) labeled units (numeric, or logical for a binary measurement, taken as 0 and 1).

x

The proxy measurement on the same \(n\) units, aligned with y.

x_unlabeled

The proxy measurement on the units of the pool that have no target value, \(N = M - n\) of them, where \(M\) is the size of the pool.

conf_level

Confidence level (default 0.95).

method

"regression" (default), the regression estimator above; or "prediction_powered", the prediction-powered estimate of Angelopoulos et al. (2023), which gives the proxy the fixed weight \(\lambda = 1\), the row proxy_weight (see Details).

cluster, cluster_unlabeled

Optional cluster identifiers for the labeled and the unlabeled units (for example the respondent who contributed several units, or the prompt that generated several items), supplied together or not at all. When given, the standard error is computed from the cluster totals of each unit's contribution to the estimate, and the limits use the t distribution on \(Q_n - 1\) degrees of freedom, where \(Q_n\) is the number of clusters among the labeled units (see Details).

Value

A data.frame (class dmar_tbl), its method attribute naming the method, with rows

mean_Y

the estimate of \(\mu_Y\), the population mean of the target.

se, df

its standard error and the degrees of freedom of the t reference distribution.

ci_lower, ci_upper

the confidence limits.

slope

the least squares slope \(\hat b\) of the target on the proxy in the labeled units. The regression estimate applies it; the prediction-powered estimate does not, and the row is reported for comparison (NA when the proxy is constant on the labeled units).

proxy_weight

the weight \(\lambda\) the estimate gives the proxy mean of the unlabeled units: \(\hat b N / M\) for the regression estimate and 1 for the prediction-powered estimate.

correlation

the correlation of target and proxy in the labeled units.

proxy_bias

the proxy mean minus the target mean in the labeled units, the proxy's bias when the two share a scale. It does not enter the regression estimate.

se_ratio_target_only

the standard error divided by that of the labeled units' target mean alone (\(s_Y/\sqrt n\), or its cluster counterpart), so values below 1 are the precision the proxy buys.

n_labeled, n_pool

the numbers of labeled units and of units in the pool, \(n\) and \(M\).

Details

The estimand. The interval is for \(\mu_Y\), the mean of the target measurement in the population from which the pool was drawn at random, the labeled units being a simple random subsample of the pool. The proxy enters only as a covariate. It need not be on the target's scale, unbiased for it, or even measured in its units, and whatever its bias, that bias does not enter the estimate; what the proxy contributes is its correlation \(\rho\) with the target. In the evaluation of a system whose outputs an automated judge labels, for example, the target is a human assessor's label of an output, the proxy is the judge's label of the same output, and the pool is the set of outputs the judge labels.

Standard error. To first order, $$\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\mu}_Y) = \frac{\sigma_Y^2 (1 - \rho^2)}{n} + \frac{\rho^2 \sigma_Y^2}{M},$$ the first term the residual variation the regression leaves among the \(n\) labeled units and the second the sampling variation of the pool itself. The reported standard error estimates \(\sigma_e^2/n + \beta^2\sigma_X^2/M\), with the residual mean square of the target on the proxy in the labeled units (on \(n - 2\) degrees of freedom) for \(\sigma_e^2\) and \(\hat b^2\) times the proxy's variance over the whole pool for \(\beta^2 \sigma_X^2\), and the limits use the t distribution on the \(n - 2\) degrees of freedom of the first term, which dominates when the pool is large. If the pool is itself the whole population of interest, a fixed collection of units every one of which carries the proxy, the estimand is the pool's own target mean and the reported standard error is conservative for it: the second term is then not needed, and the first can be multiplied by \(1 - n/M\).

Relation to prediction-powered inference. Writing \(\bar x_N\) for the proxy mean of the unlabeled units, \(\hat{\mu}_Y = \lambda \bar x_N + (\bar y_n - \lambda \bar x_n)\) with \(\lambda = \hat b N / M\). With \(\lambda = 1\) in its place this is the prediction-powered estimate of Angelopoulos et al. (2023): the proxy mean of the unlabeled units, corrected by the mean target-minus-proxy difference of the labeled units. That estimate is unbiased for any proxy, but it uses the proxy efficiently only when the proxy is on the target's scale with a slope near one, while the regression estimator learns the weight from the data; the proxy_weight row reports \(\lambda\), the weight each method applied. method = "prediction_powered" reports the interval with standard error \(\{s_{Y - X}^2/n + s_{X,N}^2/N\}^{1/2}\) and the t distribution on \(n - 1\) degrees of freedom; Angelopoulos et al. state it with the normal quantile, which the t interval approaches as \(n\) grows.

Clusters. With cluster and cluster_unlabeled, each unit's contribution to the linearized estimate is summed within its cluster, and the standard error is \(\{Q_n/(Q_n - 1) \sum_q T_q^2\}^{1/2}\), the sum running over every cluster of the pool, \(T_q\) the total of cluster \(q\), and \(Q_n\) the number of clusters among the labeled units. For the regression estimate a labeled unit contributes \(e_i/n + \hat b(x_i - \bar x_M)/M\) and an unlabeled unit \(\hat b(x_j - \bar x_M)/M\), where \(e_i\) is its residual; for the prediction-powered estimate a labeled unit contributes its target-minus-proxy difference less the mean difference, over \(n\), and an unlabeled unit its proxy less \(\bar x_N\), over \(N\). The term that dominates the variance, the residual term, comes from the labeled clusters alone, so they, and not all the clusters of the pool, set both the degrees of freedom, \(Q_n - 1\), and the small-sample factor \(Q_n/(Q_n - 1)\). When the labeled units come from a few clusters this matters: the interval then rests on those few, however many clusters the pool has. With one unit per cluster the labeled part of the prediction-powered standard error reduces to \(s_{Y - X}^2/n\), its form without clusters. At least two labeled clusters are required.

A constant proxy or target. The regression estimate needs both measurements to vary among the labeled units. A proxy that takes one value there leaves the slope undefined, and a target that takes one value (a binary target that is 1 on every labeled unit, for example) makes the residual variation and the slope both zero, so the interval would have zero width. Each is refused with an error rather than reported as an interval; more labeled units are the remedy. The prediction-powered estimate does not rest on the regression and is defined in both cases.

Missing values. A labeled unit enters only when its target, its proxy, and (if given) its cluster are all present, and an unlabeled unit only when its proxy (and cluster) is present; the others are set aside, which leaves the design intact when values are missing completely at random. The n_labeled and n_pool rows count the units used.

References

Angelopoulos, A. N., Bates, S., Fannjiang, C., Jordan, M. I., & Zrnic, T. (2023). Prediction-powered inference. Science, 382(6671), 669–674. doi:10.1126/science.adi6000

Neyman, J. (1938). Contribution to the theory of sampling human populations. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 33(201), 101–116. doi:10.1080/01621459.1938.10503378

See also

ss_aipe_two_phase and ss_aipe_two_phase_cost to plan the numbers of labeled and pool units, ss_aipe_two_phase_sensitivity to evaluate a plan, and ss_seq_two_phase for the sequential rule that needs no planning values.

Other confidence intervals: ci_crossed(), ci_proportion(), ci_proportion_paired()

Author

Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu

Examples

# A brief screening scale (the proxy) is scored for all 2,000
# respondents of a survey; a structured interview (the target) is given
# to a random 150 of them.
set.seed(113)
screen    <- rnorm(2000, mean = 50, sd = 10)
interview <- 20 + 0.6 * screen + rnorm(2000, sd = 5)
labeled   <- sample(2000, 150)
ci_two_phase(y = interview[labeled], x = screen[labeled],
             x_unlabeled = screen[-labeled])
#>  term                 value 
#>  mean_Y               51.045
#>  se                   0.405 
#>  df                   148   
#>  ci_lower             50.245
#>  ci_upper             51.845
#>  slope                0.608 
#>  proxy_weight         0.562 
#>  correlation          0.801 
#>  proxy_bias           -0.055
#>  se_ratio_target_only 0.637 
#>  n_labeled            150   
#>  n_pool               2000  
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%

# The screener is not on the interview's scale: the interview rises
# about 0.6 points per screener point. The prediction-powered estimate
# gives the screener a weight of 1 regardless, so it stays unbiased but
# its interval is wider than the regression estimator's.
ci_two_phase(y = interview[labeled], x = screen[labeled],
             x_unlabeled = screen[-labeled],
             method = "prediction_powered")
#>  term                 value 
#>  mean_Y               50.387
#>  se                   0.552 
#>  df                   149   
#>  ci_lower             49.295
#>  ci_upper             51.478
#>  slope                0.608 
#>  proxy_weight         1     
#>  correlation          0.801 
#>  proxy_bias           -0.055
#>  se_ratio_target_only 0.869 
#>  n_labeled            150   
#>  n_pool               2000  
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%
